questions.commandDemand: Give the reason. Base it on the defining characteristic of the group.
questions.stimulus: A student says that a whale is a fish because it lives in the sea and has fins.
questions.stem: Explain why the student is wrong. Explain also why living in water and having fins are not useful characteristics for classifying an animal.

fuzzyTraps.vague: a whale is not a fish
fuzzyTraps.precise: a whale is a mammal, not a fish
it breathes using lungs, while fish breathe using gills

chain.text: A whale is a mammal, not a fish.
It breathes using lungs, whereas fish breathe using gills.
It gives birth to its young alive and feeds them on milk.
Animals from several different groups live in water and have fins, so those features do not separate the groups.

questions.modelAnswer: A whale is a mammal, not a fish. A whale breathes using lungs and must come to the surface for air, while a fish breathes using gills to take in oxygen dissolved in water. A whale also gives birth to its young alive and feeds them on milk, whereas most fish lay eggs. Living in water and having fins are not useful for classifying an animal because animals from several different groups share them: fish, mammals such as whales and dolphins, and reptiles such as turtles all live in water. A characteristic is only useful for classification if it separates one group from another.
markPoints: A whale is a mammal, identified by breathing with lungs
It gives birth to young alive and feeds them milk, unlike fish
Animals from several different groups live in water and have fins
A useful characteristic must separate one group from another
questions.whyMarksLost: The second half is the real science. Classification works on characteristics that divide, not on where an animal happens to live.

questions.commandDemand: Use the table to place the animal, and say which characteristic decided it.
questions.stimulus:
Four animals were examined and their characteristics recorded.

Animal W: body covered in scales, lays eggs on land, breathes with lungs
Animal X: body covered in feathers, lays eggs, breathes with lungs
Animal Y: moist skin, lays eggs in water, young breathe with gills and adults with lungs
Animal Z: body covered in hair, gives birth to young alive, breathes with lungs
questions.stem: Infer which group each of the four animals belongs to, and state the characteristic you used for each.

fuzzyTraps.precise: Y is an amphibian, shown by the young breathing with gills and adults with lungs

chain.text: Scales and eggs laid on land, so W is a reptile.
Feathers, so X is a bird.
Moist skin with young breathing by gills and adults by lungs, so Y is an amphibian.
Hair and gives birth to young alive, so Z is a mammal.

questions.modelAnswer: Animal W is a reptile, because its body is covered in scales and it lays eggs on land. Animal X is a bird, because its body is covered in feathers. Animal Y is an amphibian, because its young breathe using gills in water while the adults breathe using lungs on land. Animal Z is a mammal, because its body is covered in hair and it gives birth to its young alive.
markPoints: All four groups correctly named
W and X justified by scales and by feathers
Y justified by the change from gills to lungs, not merely by living in water
Z justified by hair and giving birth to young alive
questions.whyMarksLost: One decisive characteristic per animal is what is wanted. Listing three features for one animal and none for another loses marks you had already earned.

questions.commandDemand: Offer a question that splits the group, and say why it works.
questions.stimulus: A student is building a dichotomous key to separate four animals: a snake, a sparrow, a goldfish and a rabbit.
questions.stem: Suggest a suitable first question for the key, explain why it is a good first question, and state one question that would be unsuitable and why.

fuzzyTraps.precise: ask about an observable characteristic that every animal either has or does not have

chain.text: Does the animal have a body covered in feathers?
It splits the group with a clear yes or no, using an observable characteristic.
A question such as 'is it big?' depends on opinion, so different people would sort the animals differently.

questions.modelAnswer: A suitable first question is: does the animal have a body covered in feathers? It is a good first question because it can only be answered yes or no, so it separates the animals into two clear groups, and it is based on an observable characteristic rather than an opinion, so everyone using the key sorts the animals the same way. A question such as 'is the animal big?' would be unsuitable, because big is relative and different people would answer it differently for the same animal.
markPoints: A question dividing the animals into two groups with a yes or no answer
Reason: it uses an observable characteristic, so the answer is not a matter of opinion
An unsuitable question named, with the reason that it is relative or a matter of opinion
questions.whyMarksLost: The third mark rewards knowing why bad keys fail. Relative words are the trap the examiner is testing for.

questions.commandDemand: State a similarity and a difference, mentioning both groups in each point.

fuzzyTraps.precise: fungi do not contain chlorophyll, so they cannot photosynthesise
fungi obtain food from dead or decaying matter

chain.text: Both fungi and green plants are living things that grow and reproduce.
Green plants contain chlorophyll and make their own food by photosynthesis.
Fungi have no chlorophyll and obtain food from dead or decaying matter.

questions.modelAnswer: Both fungi and green plants are living things which grow, reproduce and respond to their surroundings. However, green plants contain chlorophyll and can make their own food by photosynthesis, while fungi do not contain chlorophyll and cannot photosynthesise. Fungi instead obtain their food from dead or decaying matter.
markPoints: Similarity: both are living things showing characteristics such as growth and reproduction
Difference: plants have chlorophyll and photosynthesise, fungi do not and feed on dead or decaying matter
questions.whyMarksLost: Chlorophyll is the term the mark scheme hangs on. 'Fungi cannot make food' is true but does not say why.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using the defining feature of the group.
questions.stimulus: A bat flies and has wings. A student classifies it in the same group as a sparrow.
questions.stem: Explain why the bat and the sparrow belong to different groups, and state which group each belongs to.

fuzzyTraps.vague: a bat is not a bird
fuzzyTraps.precise: a bat is a mammal because its body is covered in hair and it gives birth to young alive

chain.text: The bat is a mammal and the sparrow is a bird.
The bat has hair and gives birth to its young alive.
The sparrow has feathers and lays eggs.
Animals from several groups fly, so flight does not place them together.

questions.modelAnswer: The bat is a mammal while the sparrow is a bird. The bat's body is covered in hair and it gives birth to its young alive and feeds them on milk. The sparrow's body is covered in feathers and it lays eggs. Animals are classified by these characteristics, not by whether they can fly. Insects, birds and some mammals all fly, so flying does not place two animals in the same group.
markPoints: Bat identified as a mammal by hair and giving birth to young alive
Sparrow identified as a bird by feathers and laying eggs
Flying is not a classifying characteristic, as animals from different groups fly
questions.whyMarksLost: The third mark answers the student's actual mistake. Both halves of a comparison need evidence, and the reason the wrong idea is wrong needs saying.

questions.commandDemand: State the outcome and give the reason from the characteristics of living things.
questions.stimulus: A student places some bread in a sealed damp container and leaves it in a warm dark cupboard for one week.
questions.stem: Predict what the student will observe on the bread after one week, and explain why.

fuzzyTraps.precise: mould, which is a fungus, will grow on the bread

chain.text: Mould will grow on the bread.
Mould spores in the air land on the bread.
The warm, moist and dark conditions are suitable for the spores to grow, and the bread provides food.

questions.modelAnswer: Mould will grow on the bread. Mould is a fungus, and its spores are present in the air. The cupboard is warm, damp and dark, which are suitable conditions for the spores to grow, and the bread provides the food that the mould needs. The mould will therefore grow and spread across the bread.
markPoints: Mould, identified as a fungus, will grow
Reason: warm and moist conditions plus a food source allow the spores to grow
questions.whyMarksLost: 'It will get mouldy' restates the observation. The marks are for naming mould as a fungus and for the conditions that let it grow.

questions.commandDemand: State the characteristics. No reasons needed, but they must be the ones that define living things.
questions.stimulus: A student argues that a car is alive because it moves, uses fuel and needs water.
questions.stem: Describe three characteristics of living things that a car does not have, and explain why moving and using fuel are not enough to call something living.

fuzzyTraps.vague: a car does not get bigger

chain.text: Living things grow; a car does not increase in size on its own.
Living things reproduce; a car cannot produce another car.
Living things respond to changes in their surroundings on their own.
A living thing must show all the characteristics of living things, so sharing one or two with a machine proves nothing.

questions.modelAnswer: Living things grow, but a car does not increase in size by itself. Living things reproduce to produce young of their own kind, but a car cannot produce another car. Living things respond to changes in their surroundings on their own, whereas a car only moves when a driver operates it. Moving and using fuel are not enough to call something living, because a living thing must show all of the characteristics of living things. Many non-living machines move and use fuel, so sharing one or two features with living things does not make something alive.
markPoints: Growth named as something the car does not do
Reproduction named as something the car cannot do
Responding to changes in the surroundings, or respiration, named
Explanation that a living thing must show all the characteristics, not just one or two
questions.whyMarksLost: The last mark is the argument, not another example. Something is living because it shows the whole set, and saying that is what answers the student's claim.

questions.commandDemand: Link the property of the material to the use.
questions.stimulus: The handle of a metal frying pan is made of plastic.
questions.stem: Explain why the handle is made of plastic rather than metal.

fuzzyTraps.precise: plastic is a poor conductor of heat

fuzzyTraps.vague: so you do not burn your hand
fuzzyTraps.precise: less heat is transferred to the hand, so it is safe to hold

chain.text: Plastic is a poor conductor of heat.
Heat from the pan is not easily transferred through the plastic handle.
The handle stays cool enough to hold safely.

questions.modelAnswer: Plastic is a poor conductor of heat. This means heat energy from the hot pan is not easily transferred through the handle to the person holding it. Metal is a good conductor of heat, so a metal handle would become hot quickly and could burn the hand. The plastic handle therefore stays cool enough to hold safely.
markPoints: Plastic is a poor conductor of heat
Less heat is transferred to the hand, so it can be held safely
questions.whyMarksLost: The phrase poor conductor of heat is the mark. 'Plastic does not get hot' is not accurate and does not use the property.

questions.commandDemand: Read the results and state which material suits the use, quoting the evidence.
questions.stimulus:
Four materials were tested for a raincoat. Results were recorded.

Material J: waterproof, flexible, does not tear easily
Material K: waterproof, stiff, does not tear easily
Material L: absorbs water, flexible, tears easily
Material M: waterproof, flexible, tears easily
questions.stem: Infer which material is the most suitable for making a raincoat. Give reasons for your choice and say why each of the others is unsuitable.

fuzzyTraps.precise: J is most suitable because it is waterproof, flexible and does not tear easily

chain.text: Material J is the most suitable.
It is waterproof so rain cannot pass through, flexible so it can be worn comfortably, and strong so it will not tear.
K is stiff, L absorbs water and tears, M tears easily.

questions.modelAnswer: Material J is the most suitable. It is waterproof, so rainwater cannot pass through it and the wearer stays dry. It is flexible, so it can bend and be worn comfortably. It also does not tear easily, so the raincoat will last. Material K is waterproof and strong but stiff, so it could not be worn comfortably. Material L absorbs water, so the wearer would get wet, and it tears easily. Material M is waterproof and flexible but tears easily, so it would not last.
markPoints: Material J chosen
J's waterproofness linked to keeping the wearer dry
J's flexibility and strength linked to comfort and lasting
Each rejected material linked to the property that makes it unsuitable
questions.whyMarksLost: Four marks with four materials means the rejections are worth as much as the choice. Naming J and stopping scores one.

questions.commandDemand: Offer a fair method of testing and say what would be measured.
questions.stimulus: A company wants to find out which of three fabrics is the most waterproof.
questions.stem: Suggest how the company could test the three fabrics fairly, state what would be measured, and explain how they could make the result more reliable.

fuzzyTraps.vague: pour water on them and see
fuzzyTraps.precise: pour the same volume of water onto each fabric and measure the volume that passes through

chain.text: Stretch each fabric over an identical container and pour water onto it.
Same volume of water, same pouring height, same area of fabric, same time.
Measure the volume of water that passes through each fabric.
Repeat each test several times and take the average.

questions.modelAnswer: Stretch each fabric over the top of an identical container. Pour the same volume of water from the same height onto the same area of each fabric and leave each for the same length of time. Then measure the volume of water that has collected in each container; the fabric that lets through the least water is the most waterproof. Everything except the type of fabric must be kept the same so that the test is fair. To make the result more reliable, the company should repeat the test on each fabric several times and take the average volume, so that one unusual result does not mislead them.
markPoints: A workable method using identical setups
Variables kept the same named: volume, area, height or time
The measurement stated: volume of water passing through
Repeat and average, for reliability
questions.whyMarksLost: Fairness and reliability are different marks. Keeping variables the same makes the test fair; repeating it makes the result reliable, and questions often want both.

questions.commandDemand: Link the property to the use, for both materials named.
questions.stimulus: Electrical wires are made of copper, and the covering around them is made of plastic.
questions.stem: Explain why these two materials are used.

fuzzyTraps.precise: copper is a good conductor of electricity, so current can flow through it
plastic is an insulator, so it does not allow current to pass through to the user

chain.text: Copper is a good conductor of electricity, so current flows easily along the wire.
Plastic is an insulator and does not allow current to pass through it.
The covering prevents current from reaching the user, making the wire safe to handle.

questions.modelAnswer: Copper is a good conductor of electricity, so an electric current can flow easily along the wire. Plastic is an insulator, which means it does not allow current to pass through it. The plastic covering therefore prevents the current from reaching anyone touching the wire, making it safe to handle.
markPoints: Copper is a good conductor of electricity, allowing current to flow
Plastic is an insulator, preventing current from reaching the user
questions.whyMarksLost: Both halves are required. The words conductor and insulator carry the marks; 'lets electricity through' and 'stops electricity' do not.

questions.commandDemand: State the outcome and justify it from the property tested.
questions.stimulus:
Three identical cups of hot water were each wrapped in a different material. The temperature of the water was recorded after 20 minutes.

Wrapped in wool: 62 degrees Celsius
Wrapped in cotton: 55 degrees Celsius
Wrapped in aluminium foil: 41 degrees Celsius
questions.stem: Predict which material would be best for a container to keep food warm, explain your choice using the data, and explain why the same material would also keep an ice lolly frozen for longer.

fuzzyTraps.precise: wool is the poorest conductor of heat, so the least heat is lost to the surroundings

chain.text: Wool would be the best material.
Water wrapped in wool stayed at 62 degrees Celsius, the highest of the three.
Wool is the poorest conductor of heat, so least heat energy is lost to the surroundings.
For an ice lolly the surroundings are warmer, so wool slows heat energy moving in instead.

questions.modelAnswer: Wool would be the best material. After 20 minutes the water wrapped in wool was at 62 degrees Celsius, the highest of the three, showing it lost the least heat. Wool is the poorest conductor of heat of the three materials, so the least heat energy is transferred from the water to the surroundings. The same material would keep an ice lolly frozen for longer, because in that case the surroundings are warmer than the lolly, and a poor conductor of heat also slows the transfer of heat energy from the warm surroundings into the lolly.
markPoints: Wool chosen, with the temperature evidence quoted
Wool is the poorest conductor of heat
So the least heat energy is lost to the surroundings
For the lolly, the same property slows heat energy moving in from warmer surroundings
questions.whyMarksLost: The last mark catches the idea that insulation is not about keeping heat in. It slows transfer in whichever direction the temperature difference runs.

questions.commandDemand: Give a similarity and a difference, referring to both materials each time.
questions.stem: Compare the properties of rubber and steel that make each suitable for its use in a car.

fuzzyTraps.vague: rubber is bendy and steel is hard
fuzzyTraps.precise: rubber is flexible, while steel is rigid and strong

chain.text: Both are strong enough not to break under the forces acting on a car.
Rubber is flexible and can change shape; steel is rigid and keeps its shape.
Rubber suits tyres, which must grip and absorb bumps; steel suits the body, which must hold its shape.

questions.modelAnswer: Both rubber and steel are strong, so neither breaks easily under the forces acting on a moving car. However, rubber is flexible and can change shape when a force is applied, while steel is rigid and keeps its shape. Rubber is therefore used for tyres, which must grip the road and absorb bumps, while steel is used for the body, which must keep its shape to protect the passengers.
markPoints: Similarity: both are strong
Difference: rubber is flexible while steel is rigid
Each property linked to the part of the car it suits
questions.whyMarksLost: The third mark is the link to the use. Properties listed without saying what the car needs them for answer a different question.

questions.commandDemand: State what would be observed, and the property it shows.
questions.stimulus: A student is given an unlabelled block and asked to find out whether it is made of a magnetic material.
questions.stem: Describe a test the student could carry out, state what each possible result would show, and explain why this test cannot tell her whether the block is a magnet.

fuzzyTraps.precise: observe whether the block is attracted to the magnet

chain.text: Bring a magnet close to the block.
If attracted, the block is made of a magnetic material.
If not attracted, it is not made of a magnetic material.
Attraction alone cannot show whether the block is itself a magnet; only repulsion could.

questions.modelAnswer: The student should bring a magnet close to the block and observe what happens. If the block is attracted to the magnet, it is made of a magnetic material; if it is not attracted, it is not made of a magnetic material. However, this test cannot tell her whether the block is itself a magnet, because a magnet attracts both magnetic materials and other magnets. Only repulsion would show that the block is a magnet, since only two magnets can repel each other.
markPoints: Method: bring a magnet near the block and observe
Both possible results stated with what each shows
Attraction cannot prove the block is a magnet, because a magnet also attracts a magnetic material
questions.whyMarksLost: The limitation mark is the one that matters, and it is the single most tested idea about magnets.
